pass_b_english: The saints who lived after the incarnation, having fallen asleep in faith, are superior to those who lived before. For although there were undoubtedly saints in Israel during the time of the law, with the law-given life being praised and still prevailing, those in Christ are better. They have been justified through faith and have become partakers of the divine nature, enriched with the spirit of adoption. As a result, they have been called into brotherhood by the grace of the natural and true Son.

In contrast to the spirit of slavery that existed among those under the law, we cry out 'Abba, Father' (Romans 8:15). This indicates that those in Christ are indeed better than the ancients. Our Lord Jesus Christ also implies this in the evangelical parables, where he says that the householder hires workers into the vineyard and pays them their wages, starting from the last to the first (Matthew 20:8-16). This will occur when he hands over the kingdom to God and the Father, abolishing all authority and power and might. At that time, the Son himself will also be subjected to the one who subjected all things to him, so that God may be all in all (1 Corinthians 15:28).

Some people attempt to belittle the Son by saying that he hands over the kingdom to the Father and submits to him as an inferior. However, it must be said that the Son endured a voluntary emptiness, becoming like us and humbling himself from his lofty heights, while remaining conformed and equal to the Father. He is currently hidden in God, but he will be revealed in all his glory at the time of the completion of the present age, now sitting at the right hand of the Father.

If the Son were to be brought down from his current glory, would he not undergo a second emptiness? And if he were to hand over the kingdom, how could he come with the holy angels in the glory of his Father (Matthew 25:31)? Has not the Son been given the task of putting his enemies under his feet (1 Corinthians 15:25), for now he reigns with the Father, but then he would fall from the kingdom. Nevertheless, even if the Son submits to the Father, he is not inferior to him, for submission is not a limit of nature or essence, but rather indicates a manner of action. If this were to happen among us who are not of a different essence, it would not prove difference, for a son submits to a father, a slave to a master, a student to a teacher, and someone to a leader; yet none of this injures the argument of co-essence, for they are like each other and even if they have this manner of submission, they honor each other and do not dishonor each other for the sake of harmony.

Therefore, how can they prevail over God if we are weak? For if being subject to the Son is a natural property or a measure, as they claim, then not being subject must be a property of a different nature, possibly one that is even better, given that submission is associated with lesser things. This is because he submits to God economically, for our sake.

The one who spoke in this way explained that since humanity had sinned and become subject to corruption, the devil, and demons, having departed from God by nature, the Only-Begotten became human for our sake. He abolished the power of death, removed the root of death, which is sin, and cast out the ruler of this age. Having accomplished all this and completed the entire economy, he will hand over the kingdom that was stolen long ago by others to the Father.
